To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the CO2 uptake of the synthesized porous polymers is dependent on the molecular structure of the building blocks, the conformation of the spiro-containing anhydride, and the degree of crosslinking.

(1) The CO2 adsorption capacity of the imide-based polymeric materials is dependent upon the molecular conformation of the building block monomers and the degree of crystallinity in the resulting solids, and (2) A high CO2 uptake is observed for the polymers with a high degree of crystallinity and a low degree of molecular conformational rigidity.

the spiro-containing anhydride building block and the diamine component are the most significant structural elements that can be modified to improve the CO2 sorption performance of the resultant porous solids.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the synthesis, structure-property relationships, and CO2 sorption characteristics of a series of imide-based polymeric solids with varying degrees of intrinsic microporosities and their potential as CO2 sorption materials.
the synthesis and characterization of a series of imide-based polymeric materials with varying structural diversity.

a systematic investigation of the effect of structural variations on the CO2 uptake of imide-based polymeric structures, and the relationship between structural features of the polymer and their CO2 sorption characteristics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the structural diversity of these solids is indeed a significant factor that needs to be considered for the design of efficient and effective CO2 capture systems.
the presence of a spiro ring structure within the polymer structure is a necessary requirement to obtain a high surface area and high CO2 uptake capacity.

the presence of spiro- and/or cyclohexyl moieties, as well as the incorporation of bulky substituents in the aromatic rings, are the main structural features that contribute to the generation of high surface area and high microporosity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a higher degree of structural rigidity and a higher degree of conformational flexibility of the building blocks in the solid polymer structures were both found to be favorable for the development of higher intrinsic microporosities, which in turn led to greater surface areas and higher CO2 adsorption capacities.

the presence of the spiro-containing moiety, which is capable of inducing a conformational change in the polymer chain, is a key factor in the generation of high-surface-area microporous solids, and that the incorporation of a flexible spacer group between the aromatic rings of the diamine is also important in the formation of porous solids.

a higher surface area, a greater intrinsic microporous volume, a greater microporous surface area and a lower CO2 desorption temperature were all achieved by the use of the more rigid and planar diamine building blocks.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the incorporation of spiro-bridging units in the polymeric structures of the solids can induce higher CO2 sorption capacities, and that the presence of the spiro unit in the polymeric structure is more important than the nature of the spiro-containing building blocks.
the presence of a rigid aromatic ring system in the polymer backbone is crucial for the generation of a high CO2 uptake capacity.

the presence of a conformational constraint in the building blocks of these polymers, such as a spiro linkage, is not a prerequisite to achieve high surface areas and CO2 sorption performance, but rather, it is the presence of a rigid aromatic backbone and an appropriate degree of conformational freedom of the building blocks that is critical to achieve high CO2 sorption capacity and selectivity.
